claims.text: Co-free FeNiCrMn is obtained from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi by removing Co.
Removing Co lowers the activation barrier for grain-boundary-mediated nucleation of 1/6<112> partial dislocations.
Under identical deformation conditions, Co-free FeNiCrMn will begin plastic deformation at lower strain and stress than equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
In Cantor-alloy bicrystals, grain boundaries can nucleate 1/6<112> partial dislocations.
Grain-boundary-nucleated partial dislocations propagate into the crystal and leave stacking faults.
Partial-dislocation nucleation from a grain boundary corresponds to a stress drop in the tensile stress-strain response.
The local grain-boundary structure and crystallographic loading orientation affect the energy or strain required for dislocation nucleation in the Cantor alloy.
Cantor-alloy bicrystals nucleate 1/6<112> dislocations at lower strain than corresponding single crystals.
Removing Co alters local chemical heterogeneity and lattice distortion at grain boundaries.
The Co-removal-induced change in chemical heterogeneity and lattice distortion is responsible for a reduced dislocation-nucleation barrier.
Elevating temperature from 300 K toward 1000 K softens the tested high-entropy alloys at strain rates of 10^7 to 10^9 s^-1.
Temperature and strain rate modulate the proposed Co-removal effect through thermal activation and mechanical loading.
The difference in nucleation thresholds between Co-free FeNiCrMn and equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi will become more pronounced at elevated temperature.
The Co-free alloy will show earlier stress drops and a larger stacking-fault fraction than the Cantor-alloy baseline under matched conditions.
The proposed comparison applies to tensile bicrystals containing defined grain boundaries at 300-1000 K and strain rates of 10^7 to 10^9 s^-1.
Quantitative nucleation thresholds and stress drops may depend on grain-boundary misorientation and simulation parameters.

contradictions.description: The intervention includes ballistic-impact simulations, whereas the stated boundary says the hypothesis is specific to tensile deformation in bicrystal setups.

The outcome predicts a temperature-dependent amplification but gives no directional strain-rate prediction, while the falsification rule treats absence of either temperature or strain-rate modulation as falsifying.
